title: Agreement
note: A verb agrees in number with its subject, not with a noun that happens to sit nearby. Each, either, neither, everyone and somebody are singular. With or or nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject. A pronoun agrees with its antecedent, the word it refers back to.

src.t: Purdue OWL, Making Subjects and Verbs Agree

items.ex: Phrases like 'with', 'along with' and 'as well as' do not change the subject's number.
In American usage a collective noun acting as a unit takes a singular verb.
An amount treated as one sum is singular.
'The number' is singular; 'a number' means 'several' and is plural.

read.title: Finding the true subject
text: Most agreement errors happen when something distracts the writer from the real subject. The commonest distraction is a phrase between the subject and the verb. In "The list of names is long," the verb is singular because the subject is list. The plural word names sits inside a prepositional phrase, and a noun inside such a phrase is never the subject.

Phrases such as along with, together with and as well as cause the same trouble. "The mayor, as well as her aides, is here" takes a singular verb, because the added phrase does not make the subject plural. Only and joins subjects into a plural.

Word order can also hide the subject. In sentences that begin with there or here, the subject comes after the verb: "There are three reasons," "Here is the key." Finally, with or and nor the verb agrees with whichever subject is closer to it: "Neither the coach nor the players were ready."
The fix in every case is the same. Strip away the phrases, find the word the sentence is really about, and make the verb agree with it.

q.q: Why is "The list of names is long" correct?
o: The subject is list, not names
Of always takes a singular verb

q.q: According to the reading, which word joins subjects into a plural?
In "Neither the coach nor the players were ready," why is were plural?
o: The verb agrees with the closer subject, players
The coach is a collective noun
